title: Chapter I

teacherSummary.text: The novel opens with its famous ironic line about a single man in possession of a good fortune. Mrs. Bennet excitedly tells Mr. Bennet that a wealthy young man, Mr. Bingley, has rented Netherfield Park; Mr. Bennet teases her.

vocabulary.context: Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, merely on that account, for in general you know they visit no newcomers.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “newcomer”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To free from that which infolds or envelops
vocabulary.context: Her mind was less difficult to develop.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “develop”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: An abrupt change in feeling, opinion, or action, proceeding from some whim or fancy
vocabulary.context: Bennet was so odd a mixture of quick parts, sarcastic humour, reserve, and caprice, that the experience of three and twenty years had been insufficient to make his wife understand his character.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “caprice”: cap (Latin capere, "to take"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: Bennet,” replied his wife, “how can you be so tiresome!
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “tiresome”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: To commend to the favorable notice of another
vocabulary.context: “They have none of them much to recommend them,” replied he; “they are all silly and ignorant like other girls; but Lizzy has something more of quickness than her sisters.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “recommend”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: The act of mixing, or the state of being mixed
vocabulary.context: Bennet was so odd a mixture of quick parts, sarcastic humour, reserve, and caprice, that the experience of three and twenty years had been insufficient to make his wife understand his character.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “mixture”: -ure (Latin -ura, "act, result"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: Bennet was so odd a mixture of quick parts, sarcastic humour, reserve, and caprice, that the experience of three and twenty years had been insufficient to make his wife understand his character.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “reserve”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To unite in wedlock or matrimony
vocabulary.context: You must know that I am thinking of his marrying one of them.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “marry”: mar (Latin mare, "sea"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.context: You have no compassion on my poor nerves.”
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “compassion”: com- (Latin com-, "with, together") + -sion (Latin -sio, "the act of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: I certainly have had my share of beauty, but I do not pretend to be anything extraordinary now.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “pretend”: pre- (Latin prae, "before") + ten (Latin tenere, "to hold"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

context.history: In Regency England, daughters of gentry families depended on marriage for security; the Bennet estate is entailed away from daughters.

significance: The opening sentence is among the most quoted in English and models Austen's irony: it means the reverse of what it seems to say.
discussionQuestions: What does the first sentence really suggest about who wants the marriage?
Where does irony appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with first impressions and prejudice?

items.prompt: How does Mr. Bennet treat his wife's excitement?
What is the tone of the opening sentence?
What is Mrs. Bennet's main goal?
How many daughters do the Bennets have?
In the line “Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, merely on that account, for in general you know they visit no newcomers.”, what does “newcomers” most nearly mean?
options: An abrupt change in feeling, opinion, or action, proceeding from some whim or fancy
To free from that which infolds or envelops

items.prompt: In the line “Her mind was less difficult to develop.”, what does “develop” most nearly mean?
options: An abrupt change in feeling, opinion, or action, proceeding from some whim or fancy
To free from that which infolds or envelops

answerKey.answer: To free from that which infolds or envelops

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter I,” how does Austen show marriage as a social goal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: High School / Common Core
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter I develops the idea of marriage as a social goal. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of irony and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses irony in Chapter I to complicate the reader's understanding of marriage as a social goal. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter I within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of marriage as a social goal responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter I as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of marriage as a social goal. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter I”?

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true
annotationFocus.passage: “My dear, you flatter me. I certainly have had my share of beauty, but I do not pretend to be anything extraordinary now. When a woman has five grown up daughters, she ought to give over thinking of her own beauty.”

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them

annotationFocus.label: Tone / mood
annotationFocus.lookFor: word choices that reveal the narrator's attitude or the scene's feeling

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does the first sentence really suggest about who wants the marriage? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are newcomers, develop, caprice, tiresome, recommend. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go, merely on that account, for in general you know they visit no newcomers.” Webster's says: One who has lately come. Now the word history: “newcomer”: -er (Old English -ere, "one who"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “develop”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “caprice”: cap (Latin capere, "to take"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. In Regency England, daughters of gentry families depended on marriage for security; the Bennet estate is entailed away from daughters. Why does this chapter matter? The opening sentence is among the most quoted in English and models Austen's irony: it means the reverse of what it seems to say. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for irony.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see irony, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to marriage as a social goal.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of irony. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: “My dear, you flatter me. I certainly have had my share of beauty, but I do not pretend to be anything extraordinary now. When a woman has five grown up daughters, she ought to give over thinking of her own beauty.”

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Irony, Characterization, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter I,” how does Austen show marriage as a social goal? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the irony you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about marriage as a social goal, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how irony shapes marriage as a social goal. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
